Name: Login
Description of item/issue: Focus indicators for actionable elements must be present and meet contrast requirements.
Recommended Fix:
A focus indicator must always be visible and have at least 3:1 contrast.

It is best to intentionally style the focus indicator for all links, buttons, fields, etc. We encourage you to change the shape somehow (add a border, box, underline, etc.) as well as choose a color that has sufficient contrast with either the background of the page (if placed outside of the element) or the element itself (if placed inside of the element).

Name: Login
Description of item/issue: Errors are not identified to screen reader users.
Recommended Fix:
Ensure that screen reader users are informed of the errors present for these form fields.

There are a number of ways that this can be addressed. Ideally, add an `aria-describedby` attribute and set focus on the first form field with an error. The `aria-describedby` attribute should be placed on the affected form field. It takes the `ID` of the element that contains the description of the error. If the form field is described by more than one element, you can set the `aria-describedby` attribute to a space-separated list of IDs.

Some alternative approaches are the following:

* Add an `aria-invalid` attribute to the `<input>` elements with errors. Ideally this is accompanied by setting focus on the first `<input>` with an error.
* Utilize the browser error alerts to indicate this information.

Once you have decided which type of tooltip to implement (manual or automatic), please make a comment on this issue to let us know, and then include this issue in an upcoming QA or reach out to your CSM to have this content audited. 1. Add a heading (preferably an `<h1>`, but `<h2>` is acceptable), then associate it with the modal dialog wrapper by giving that heading a unique `id` and referencing it with an `aria-labelledby` attribute on the wrapper element (the element with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`).

1. Alternatively, add an `aria-label` attribute to the wrapper element (the element with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`) describing the purpose of the modal dialog.

Name: Home
Description of item/issue: Content changes are not announced as users enter text in the live filter input.

Name: Home
Description of item/issue: Keyboard users are unable to interact with these tabs as expected.
Recommended Fix:
Keyboard and screen reader users will expect to be able to interact with these tabs in the following ways:

1. Only the currently selected tab should be focusable via the tab key. To do this, add a `tabindex="-1"` to all non-selected tabs.
1. Ensure that the `Left` and `Right` arrow keys allow the user to traverse the options in the tablist.
1. Tabs can be activated automatically or manually. If they are activated automatically, the tabs will be selected as they are traversed via the arrow keys. If they are activated manually, they will be selected by pressing either the `Enter` or `Space` key. Ensure that the `aria-selected` and `tabindex` attributes are updated as the new tab is activated. See this [section about automatic versus manual activation](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/606#heading-automatic-versus-manual-tab-activation) in the related Knowledge Base article to learn more.

If these tabs are arranged vertically, ensure that users can use the `Up` and `Down` arrow keys (in addition to `Left` and `Right`) to traverse the tabs.

Optionally, you may additionally choose to allow users to use the `Home` and `End` keys to navigate to the start and end of the tablist.

To do so, target the `ID` of the `<main>` tag, or fire a `.focus()` event on that element so screen reader users begin reading the page from there. The element receiving focus will need a `tabindex` of `-1`, or will need to be natively focusable by the browser.

Recommended Fix: Add screen reader only text inside of the filter region, and before the input, that [provides instructions](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/922#heading-instructions-for-screen-reader-users) on how to use this live filter. Extend this screen reader only statement with additional instructional text tailored to your content and functionality as needed.

Name: Home
Description of item/issue: This live filter region requires additional ARIA markup to assist screen reader users in understanding what this section is for, and where it begins and ends.
Recommended Fix:
Wrap both the text field and the content that it filters in a `<section>` tag or a `<div>` with `role=“region”` so that screen reader users can tell that they are related. 

Give this wrapper element a generic `aria-label` attribute value that broadly identifies what kind of content is being filtered. For example, “location filter” or “product filter”. 

See the [wrapper markup section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/922#heading-wrapper) of the Knowledge Base article on Live Filters.

Name: Home
Description of item/issue: Content changes are not announced as users enter text in the live filter input.
Recommended Fix: Use a “live region” to announce when the filtered content changes as the user types in the text field. To accomplish this, add a visually hidden container, and give this container the `aria-live=”assertive”` attribute. When results are found, insert text into this container similar to "[#] results available". When no results are found, insert text like "no results available" so that users know that they should probably stop typing and try a different search term.

Name: Home
Description of item/issue: When content is marked up as a heading, but is not semantically a heading, it can be confusing for screen reader users.
Recommended Fix:
Remove the heading markup, then verify the page maintains a logical outline structure without skipping any heading levels. For example,

- An `<h2>` should head each major section of the page.
- Subsequent heading levels (`<h3>` through `<h6>`) should be related to a parent heading level that is one level higher.

---

Please see these Knowledge Base articles for [heading levels](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/74) and [text that is not a heading](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/101) for more information about heading level structure.

Name: Home
Description of item/issue: When a table column can be sorted, this must be indicated to screen reader users.
Recommended Fix: Add an `aria-sort` attribute to the currently-sorted column’s `<th>` tag, then ensure the attribute's value is "ascending" when sorted from A to Z and "descending" when the column is sorted from Z to A. If the column is unsorted, remove the attribute, as the `aria-sort` attribute should exist on only one table header at a time.

Description of item/issue: Text within images causes problems for screen reader users and users who require high contrast or screen magnification, but it appears that you have taken steps to mitigate this fact.
Recommended Fix:
Recreating this text with HTML and CSS is likely to be difficult; however it appears you’ve taken steps to mitigate this issue by providing appropriate `alt` text for the image, and ensuring that the image is reasonably readable up to 200% zoom. **Please note**, this method does not fully meet the requirements of WCAG 2.0 Success Criterion 1.4.5 "Image of Text", but as a P3 level issue, it will not prevent you from receiving a Letter of Conformance. If you choose to not make any further changes, we will close this issue as "Not Fixing".

**There are two options for remediating this in a way that fully meets WCAG requirements:**

- Extract the text from the image and place it on the page using HTML; use CSS to style and position it as desired superimposed over the image(s).
_Or…_
- Place the text on the page adjacent to the image, similar to a caption.

**Reminder:** When overlaying text on an image, make sure the [text has proper contrast](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/862#heading-text-over-images-and-complex-backgrounds) to the background image.

* If the top-level navigation item only actuates a menu and **does not** navigate to a new page when activated, mark it up as a button (`<button>`). See [this code sample](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/529#heading-menubar-where-menu-triggers-are-buttons) for guidance.

* If styling constraints do not allow for a visible button, this button could be visually hidden by default and become visible only when receiving focus, as shown in this [code sample](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/529#heading-menubar-where-menu-triggers-use-a-link-and-a-button-that-becomes-visible-on-focus).

Name: Project Details
Description of item/issue: Text that functions as a heading should be marked up as such.
Recommended Fix:
Mark this text up as a heading.

Headings provide structure for screen reader users. When marking text up as a heading, verify that the page maintains a logical outline structure. For example; 

- Each page needs a single `<h1>` heading that describes the main purpose of the page.
- An `<h2>` should head each major section of the page.
- Subsequent heading levels (`<h3>` through `<h6>`) should be related to a parent `<h2>` and should not skip heading levels.

Name: Project Details
Description of item/issue: Tooltip content must be reachable by all users, including screen reader and keyboard users.
Recommended Fix:
Making tooltips accessible can be accomplished in two distinct ways:

- Make your tooltips accessible by using **manually**-activated tooltips. Please see [this section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/524#heading-for-manuallyactivated-tooltips) in the Tooltips Knowledge Base article.
- Make your tooltips accessible by using **automatically**-activated tooltips. Please see [this section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/524#heading-for-automaticallyactivated-tooltips) in the Tooltips Knowledge Base article.
  - **Note:** If you elect to use automatically-activated tooltips, these tooltips must convert to manually-activated tooltips when they are displayed on smaller viewports with a responsive layout. Please see the section regarding [Tooltip that is only available on smaller viewports](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/524#heading-tooltip-that-is-only-available-on-smaller-viewports) for more information on mobile responsive tooltips and a code sample illustrating this functionality.

Once you have decided which type of tooltip to implement (manual or automatic), please make a comment on this issue to let us know, and then include this issue in an upcoming QA or reach out to your CSM to have this content audited. We will then set this issue to Not Applicable and add new issues as needed to address the content.

Description of item/issue: Images that lack alt attributes make it impossible for screen reader users to know what the image depicts.
Recommended Fix:
Ensure each image has an `alt` attribute. The content of the alt attribute depends on the image type.

If an image is **informative** (i.e. provides information not conveyed in other ways), add an `alt` attribute to the image which conveys the information provided by it.
If an image is **decorative** (i.e. does not contribute any meaningful information), give the image an empty `alt` attribute (`alt=“”`).

For more advice on determining which images are decorative or informative, visit our Knowledge Base Article: [The Art of Alt Attributes](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/472).

1. Add a heading (preferably an `<h1>`, but `<h2>` is acceptable), then associate it with the modal dialog wrapper by giving that heading a unique `id` and referencing it with an `aria-labelledby` attribute on the wrapper element (the element with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`).

  * This heading is most helpful when it is visible for all users, but for strict WCAG conformance it can be made visible only to screen reader users instead.
1. Alternatively, add an `aria-label` attribute to the wrapper element (the element with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`) describing the purpose of the modal dialog.

Recommended Fix:
Add `role="listbox"` to the `<ul>` containing the results. Add an `aria-labelledby` attribute to the `<ul>`. The `aria-labelledby` attribute takes the ID of the `<label>` associated with the autocomplete's text input field.

Next, add `role="option"` to each `<li>`. Ensure that each of these list items has a unique `id` attribute value.

See [this section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/427#heading-simple-listbox-popup) of the Autocompletes Knowledge Base article for additional guidance.

Name: Processes
Description of item/issue: This text input with autocomplete functionality is missing critical ARIA attributes.
Recommended Fix:

Additionally, if a list popup is used:

1. Add `aria-controls="[ID of list element]"`.
1. Add `aria-haspopup="listbox"`.
1. Add `aria-expanded` and set its value to `true` or `false` based on the visibility of the list. Update this value as necessary as the user interacts with the autocomplete.

See [this section of the Autocompletes KB article](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/427#heading-text-input) for complete guidance on marking up this text input as an autocomplete.

Name: Processes

Recommended Fix:

Follow [the guidance in this section of the Autocompletes KB article](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/427#heading-results-found-announcements-for-screen-reader-users) for how to make this information available for screen reader users. 

Additionally, refer to the [Listbox Popup code sample](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/427#heading-listbox-popup).

Recommended Fix:

Recommended Fix:

* Add the attribute `aria-labelledby` to the element with `role=”tabpanel”` and set its value equal to the `id` of the tab element that controls it.

Name: Processes
Description of item/issue: Keyboard users are unable to interact with these tabs as expected.
Recommended Fix:
Keyboard and screen reader users will expect to be able to interact with these tabs in the following ways:

1. Only the currently selected tab should be focusable via the tab key. To do this, add a `tabindex="-1"` to all non-selected tabs.
1. Ensure that the `Left` and `Right` arrow keys allow the user to traverse the options in the tablist.
1. Tabs can be activated automatically or manually. If they are activated automatically, the tabs will be selected as they are traversed via the arrow keys. If they are activated manually, they will be selected by pressing either the `Enter` or `Space` key. Ensure that the `aria-selected` and `tabindex` attributes are updated as the new tab is activated. See this [section about automatic versus manual activation](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/606#heading-automatic-versus-manual-tab-activation) in the related Knowledge Base article to learn more.

If these tabs are arranged vertically, ensure that users can use the `Up` and `Down` arrow keys (in addition to `Left` and `Right`) to traverse the tabs.

Optionally, you may additionally choose to allow users to use the `Home` and `End` keys to navigate to the start and end of the tablist.

Name: Add Event
Affected item: "Date and Time:" fields > time autocomplete results
Description of item/issue: These autocomplete results are missing critical ARIA attributes.
Recommended Fix:
Add `role="listbox"` to the `<ul>` containing the results. Add an `aria-labelledby` attribute to the `<ul>`. The `aria-labelledby` attribute takes the ID of the `<label>` associated with the autocomplete's text input field.

Next, add `role="option"` to each `<li>`. Ensure that each of these list items has a unique `id` attribute value.

See [this section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/427#heading-simple-listbox-popup) of the Autocompletes Knowledge Base article for additional guidance.

If a popup listbox is used in addition to the inline autocomplete, add `aria-autocomplete="both"` to the input text field. 

See [this section of the Autocompletes KB article](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/427#heading-inline-suggestions) for more guidance.

Name: Add Event

Additionally, if a list popup is used:

1. Add `aria-controls="[ID of list element]"`.
1. Add `aria-haspopup="listbox"`.
1. Add `aria-expanded` and set its value to `true` or `false` based on the visibility of the list. Update this value as necessary as the user interacts with the autocomplete.

See [this section of the Autocompletes KB article](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/427#heading-text-input) for complete guidance on marking up this text input as an autocomplete.

Description of item/issue: The information contained in charts or graphs may not be accessible for all users.
Recommended Fix:
Charts or graphs that rely on visual appearance (such as color alone) to convey meaning, may not convey that information to color blind and screen reader users. 

**For color blind users:**
Ensure that information is not conveyed by color alone, and has a second visual indicator, such as shape, outlining, etc. (See the [Charts and graphs section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/863#heading-charts-and-graphs) of this article for more information.)

**For screen reader users:**
Add a table for screen reader users which communicates the same information provided by the graph. You might also consider making the table visible to everyone, and not just to screen reader users, as other users may benefit from having this information presented in another way.

Description of item/issue: Text within images causes problems for screen reader users and users of magnification technology.
Recommended Fix:
**Preferred Remediation:**

- Extract the text from the image and place it on the page using HTML; use CSS to style and position it as desired superimposed over the image(s).
_Or…_
- Place the text on the page adjacent to the image, similar to a caption.

**Alternative Remediation:**

We recognize solving this issue using the preferred method may not be feasible for all situations, so completing all of the numbered steps is an alternative solution to close this issue: 

1. Add all of the text from the image, and [any other visual information necessary for understanding](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/472), to an `alt` attribute on the image. If the `alt` attribute is already present, ensure it accurately reflects the text within the image and that the other steps for this recommendation are followed.
1. Ensure that the image is reasonably readable up to 200% zoom.
1. (Optional) Add only the text from the image as a title attribute to the image to assist magnification users.

**Reminder:** When overlaying text on an image, make sure the [text has proper contrast](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/862#heading-text-over-images-and-complex-backgrounds) to the background image. 

Please note, this method will not meet WCAG 1.4.5, but it has been determined to be an acceptable exception to resolve this issue. **By choosing the “Alternative Remediation” method described above you are accepting any accessibility liability risk for this content and understand that this remediation option does not comply with the associated WCAG guidelines which will continue to present some accessibility issues.**

After this alternative remediation has been successfully implemented, we will downgrade this issue to a warning (P3) with a comment indicating as such and set the issue status to Not Fixing. This status will not prevent you from obtaining a Letter of Conformance and it is encouraged that you attempt to fully remediate this content using the preferred remediation methods during future updates.

All of the following solutions are acceptable, and you are free to decide which solution feels the most "appropriate" to you in this use case.

1. To the close (X) button, if one is used.
1. To the visible heading that labels the modal dialog, if one is used.
1. To the modal dialog wrapper itself (the element with both `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`).
1. To the primary call to action (CTA) element (such as an "OK" button), or the element for the least destructive action in a set of CTAs (like "Cancel" next to a button for "Delete").

  * This heading is most helpful when it is visible for all users, but for strict WCAG conformance it can be made visible only to screen reader users instead.
1. Alternatively, add an `aria-label` attribute to the wrapper element (the element with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`) describing the purpose of the modal dialog.

Name: Delete Report
Description of item/issue: The modal dialog container is not labeled.
Recommended Fix:
Provide a [label using one of the following methods](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/820#heading-labelling). All of these solutions are acceptable, but some may be easier to implement than others depending on the content within the modal dialog.

1. Add a heading (preferably an `<h1>`, but `<h2>` is acceptable), then associate it with the modal dialog wrapper by giving that heading a unique `id` and referencing it with an `aria-labelledby` attribute on the wrapper element (the element with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`).
  * If a heading describing the contents of the modal dialog already exists, you can use that heading instead.
  * This heading is most helpful when it is visible for all users, but for strict WCAG conformance it can be made visible only to screen reader users instead.
1. Alternatively, add an `aria-label` attribute to the wrapper element (the element with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`) describing the purpose of the modal dialog.

Name: Delete Report
Description of item/issue: Keyboard and screen reader users do not have their focus moved to this modal dialog when it opens.
Recommended Fix:
Set the keyboard focus to the [most appropriate element](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/820#heading-moving-focus-into-a-modal-dialog-when-it-opens) inside this modal dialog, depending on the content it contains. All of the following solutions are acceptable, and you are free to decide which solution feels the most "appropriate" to you in this use case.

1. To the close (X) button, if one is used.
1. To the visible heading that labels the modal dialog, if one is used.
1. To the modal dialog wrapper itself (the element with both `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`).
1. To the primary call to action (CTA) element (such as an "OK" button), or the element for the least destructive action in a set of CTAs (like "Cancel" next to a button for "Delete").

**Note:** in order to set focus on an element that cannot natively receive focus (like a heading or the wrapper element), add the attribute `tabindex="-1"` to it.

**Preferred Remediation:**

- Extract the text from the image and place it on the page using HTML; use CSS to style and position it as desired superimposed over the image(s).
_Or…_

1. Ensure that the image is reasonably readable up to 200% zoom.
1. (Optional) Add only the text from the image as a title attribute to the image to assist magnification users.

**Reminder:** When overlaying text on an image, make sure the [text has proper contrast](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/862#heading-text-over-images-and-complex-backgrounds) to the background image.

Name: Project Details | Forms | Select a Form
Description of item/issue: Text that functions as a heading should be marked up as such.
Recommended Fix:
Mark this text up as a heading.

Headings provide structure for screen reader users. When marking text up as a heading, verify that the page maintains a logical outline structure. For example; 

- Each page needs a single `<h1>` heading that describes the main purpose of the page.
- An `<h2>` should head each major section of the page.
- Subsequent heading levels (`<h3>` through `<h6>`) should be related to a parent `<h2>` and should not skip heading levels.

Name: Dashboard Example - Budgets BI
Description of item/issue: These tab controls are missing critical ARIA attributes.
Recommended Fix:
* Add `role="tab"` to the triggering elements. 
* Add an `aria-controls` attribute to each element with the `role="tab"`. Ensure that the value of the `aria-controls` attribute is the `id` of the tabpanel it is intended to control.
* Add an `aria-selected` attribute to each of these elements as well. Set its value to "true" on the tab element that is currently active, and "false" for all other tabs. Ensure the value of this attribute is dynamically updated as the user interacts with the tabs to indicate the active tab at all times.

Name: Dashboard Example - Budgets BI
Description of item/issue: These tab panels are missing critical ARIA attributes.
Recommended Fix:
* Add `role="tabpanel"` to the container element wrapping the content controlled by the related element with `role=”tab”`.
* Add the attribute `aria-labelledby` to the element with `role=”tabpanel”` and set its value equal to the `id` of the tab element that controls it.
* Optionally, as a usability best practice, add `tabindex="0"` to each tab panel to make the component easier for inexperienced keyboard-only users to navigate.

Name: Dashboard Example - Budgets BI
Description of item/issue: Keyboard users are unable to interact with these tabs as expected.
Recommended Fix:
Keyboard and screen reader users will expect to be able to interact with these tabs in the following ways:

1. Only the currently selected tab should be focusable via the tab key. To do this, add a `tabindex="-1"` to all non-selected tabs.
1. Ensure that the `Left` and `Right` arrow keys allow the user to traverse the options in the tablist.
1. Tabs can be activated automatically or manually. If they are activated automatically, the tabs will be selected as they are traversed via the arrow keys. If they are activated manually, they will be selected by pressing either the `Enter` or `Space` key. Ensure that the `aria-selected` and `tabindex` attributes are updated as the new tab is activated. See this [section about automatic versus manual activation](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/606#heading-automatic-versus-manual-tab-activation) in the related Knowledge Base article to learn more.

If these tabs are arranged vertically, ensure that users can use the `Up` and `Down` arrow keys (in addition to `Left` and `Right`) to traverse the tabs.

Optionally, you may additionally choose to allow users to use the `Home` and `End` keys to navigate to the start and end of the tablist.

Recommended Fix:

**For color blind users:**
Ensure that information is not conveyed by color alone, and has a second visual indicator, such as shape, outlining, etc. (See the [Charts and graphs section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/863#heading-charts-and-graphs) of this article for more information.)

Name: Profile
Description of item/issue: When non-essential icons are not properly hidden from screen reader users, they can be announced as unrecognized characters.
Recommended Fix:
Hide non-essential icons by moving them into their own `<span>`, or other inline tag, then giving the `<span>` an `aria-hidden="true"` attribute.

If a non-essential icon is already independently wrapped by an element, instead give this element an `aria-hidden="true"` attribute. Ensure that no other content is contained within the element wrapping the icon, as doing so may inadvertently or improperly hide the additional content from screen reader users.

Name: Profile
Description of item/issue: Errors are not identified to screen reader users.
Recommended Fix:
Ensure that screen reader users are informed of the errors present for these form fields.

There are a number of ways that this can be addressed. Ideally, add an `aria-describedby` attribute and set focus on the first form field with an error. The `aria-describedby` attribute should be placed on the affected form field. It takes the `ID` of the element that contains the description of the error. If the form field is described by more than one element, you can set the `aria-describedby` attribute to a space-separated list of IDs.

Some alternative approaches are the following:

* Add an `aria-invalid` attribute to the `<input>` elements with errors. Ideally this is accompanied by setting focus on the first `<input>` with an error.
* Utilize the browser error alerts to indicate this information.

Name: Instance Details
Description of item/issue: Keyboard and screen reader users do not have their focus moved to this modal dialog when it opens.
Recommended Fix:
Set the keyboard focus to the [most appropriate element](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/820#heading-moving-focus-into-a-modal-dialog-when-it-opens) inside this modal dialog, depending on the content it contains. All of the following solutions are acceptable, and you are free to decide which solution feels the most "appropriate" to you in this use case.

1. To the close (X) button, if one is used.
1. To the visible heading that labels the modal dialog, if one is used.
1. To the modal dialog wrapper itself (the element with both `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`).
1. To the primary call to action (CTA) element (such as an "OK" button), or the element for the least destructive action in a set of CTAs (like "Cancel" next to a button for "Delete").

**Note:** in order to set focus on an element that cannot natively receive focus (like a heading or the wrapper element), add the attribute `tabindex="-1"` to it.

Name: Instance Details
Description of item/issue: The modal dialog container is not labeled.
Recommended Fix:
Provide a [label using one of the following methods](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/820#heading-labelling). All of these solutions are acceptable, but some may be easier to implement than others depending on the content within the modal dialog.

1. Add a heading (preferably an `<h1>`, but `<h2>` is acceptable), then associate it with the modal dialog wrapper by giving that heading a unique `id` and referencing it with an `aria-labelledby` attribute on the wrapper element (the element with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`).
  * If a heading describing the contents of the modal dialog already exists, you can use that heading instead.
  * This heading is most helpful when it is visible for all users, but for strict WCAG conformance it can be made visible only to screen reader users instead.
1. Alternatively, add an `aria-label` attribute to the wrapper element (the element with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`) describing the purpose of the modal dialog.
